summary:
Nevada stands under the United States federal framework, which governs passports, entry screening, federal custody and federal care measures; those apply within the state and are carried by the national record. The findings below are specific to Nevada.

A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places Nevada in its Low-Risk group, crediting the state with fairly robust non-discrimination policies while finding that it falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

Nevada law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public accommodation under provisions effective 1 October 2011 and extended throughout state statutes effective 1 July 2017. In November 2022 voters approved Question 1 by 58%, adding sexual orientation and gender identity or expression to the state Constitution's equal protection clause.

The state hate-crime law provides additional penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived characteristics. It was amended to add gender identity or expression after passage in May 2013, effective 1 October 2013, and a hate-crime reporting hotline was established in January 2025.

Identity documents can be changed without surgery. Since 2016 Nevada Vital Records issues a birth certificate with corrected gender on receipt of two affidavits reflecting preferred gender, and comparable changes are permitted for driver's licences and state IDs. The DMV and Vital Records offer an "X" third-gender designation on licences, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation required, available from 2019. Legislation signed 22 June 2017 abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before a legal sex change on government documents.

Gender-affirming care carries state-level protection. Health insurers are barred by state law from discriminating against transgender patients, the state Medicaid agency announced in March 2018 that it would cover sex reassignment surgery, and a bill passed in June 2023 and signed by the governor requires insurers including Medicaid to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments effective 1 January 2024. The governor vetoed the broader SB 302 omnibus in 2023, which would have shielded gender-affirming care and mandated Medicaid surgery coverage.

In May 2023 the governor approved legislation explicitly protecting transgender and intersex people within state correctional facilities. The July 2026 assessment nonetheless finds Nevada short on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 8 October 2014, when the Ninth Circuit struck down the state's marriage ban in Sevcik v. Sandoval. Voters removed the constitutional ban by approving Question 2 with 62% in November 2020, and in December 2020 the Nevada Supreme Court required retroactive recognition of out-of-state same-sex marriages performed before 2014.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 assessment places Nevada in its Low-Risk group alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, one tier below the most-protective group.

Nevada's written law mandates insurer coverage of gender-affirming care and explicitly protects transgender inmates in state custody, yet the same assessment rates the state short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people. The shortfall it identifies therefore concerns how those protections operate, not whether the statutes exist.

The inventory's comparison source for public-facility access is the Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map, which records state-by-state rules on whether transgender people may use public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity; no Nevada-specific entry from that map is carried in the inventory.
localsOnly:
Anti-bullying law SB 504, effective 1 July 2015, expressly lists gender identity or expression as a protected ground and directs school policies, reporting, parent notification and staff training.

The March 2018 Medicaid decision to cover sex reassignment surgery followed the governor's veto of a coverage mandate on 22 June 2017.

School sports eligibility tightened for residents. In April 2025 the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association reversed its 2016 policy and now requires transgender athletes to compete under their sex assigned at birth, while a governor-supported 2026 ballot initiative to generally determine school sports eligibility by sex assigned at birth failed to reach the November 2026 ballot.

Conversion therapy on minors was banned under a bill signed 17 May 2017, effective 1 January 2018. The gay panic defence was repealed by legislation signed 14 May 2019, effective 1 October 2019.

The Nevada Domestic Partnership Act, effective 1 October 2009 after a veto override, grants many marriage rights but exempts private and public employers from providing medical coverage to domestic partners, and leaves parental rights less well defined with uncertain interstate recognition.

Same-sex relationships have not been a legal barrier to adoption, state law since 2017 reflects equal parental rights, lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilisation with recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother regardless of marital status, and gestational surrogacy is permitted and recognised equally while traditional surrogacy contracts are illegal.
outOfScopeNotes:
The July 2026 assessment's findings on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people are stated qualitatively; the inventory carries no figures, incident counts or dates behind them, so the size of either shortfall is unresolved.

No Nevada-specific incident of violence against a transgender person, with a date and an outcome, appears in the inventory, so no state-level pattern of such incidents can be described from these sources.

The inventory records no Nevada-specific data on screening, pat-downs or document handling at the state's airports and ports of entry; those processes are federal and are carried by the national record.

Whether Nevada restricts transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities is not resolved here: the facilities map cited as the comparison source is named in the inventory, but no Nevada entry from it is reproduced.
